name: Enabling discovery and identification
description: To facilitate reuse of data, we need to first make data discoverable. Data discoverability involves assigning identifiers and metadata to a dataset to allow users to query, find, interpret, and reuse it. Choosing an appropriate repository, improving file structure, providing documentation, and producing machine-discoverable metadata, are all part of this process. Making data discoverable also contributes to making research more transparent and reproducible.
text:
#### Sections:
[Considerations](#considerations) | [Recommendations](#recommendations) | [More information](#more-information) | [Author](#author)

### Considerations

- Consider where to publish your data for improved discoverability; in a discipline-specific or agnostic repository, and preferably in a TDR (Trustworthy Digital Repository)
- Consider how you structure data into levels of datasets and files to decide what will be assigned an identifier and support meaningful discovery
- Consider which terms you use to describe the dataset (e.g., title, abstract, metadata) to make them align with a user’s search terms
- Consider what a user will need to know to be able to interpret and reuse a dataset, and include necessary information together with the dataset

### Recommendations

- Datasets should be assigned unique, persistent identifiers (PIDs) (REC-12)
- Use PIDs on both dataset and file level (FRM-08)
- Data should be well documented (e.g., clear explanations, metadata, readme files) (REC-05)
- Provide machine-discoverable and interpretable metadata about both deposits (identifiers, authorship) and deposit content (quality, experimental conditions, variables measured) (FRM-07)

### More Information
This module builds upon the following supporting frameworks:
- CoreTrustSeal_v1: R10; R12
- Core Preservation Processes (CPPs): 005; 009; 011; 013; 016; 019; 021; 024; 028
- EOSC-A TF FAIR Metrics and Digital Objects: FRM-07; FRM-08
- RDMkit Elixir-Europe: Data discoverability


### Author

Camilla Hagen Blixhavn, https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9560-1690

name: Reviewing deposits - file formats and technical data quality
description:
For a data repository manager, technical data quality is primarily about whether the deposited files are technically sound, complete, usable, and suitable for long-term preservation and reuse. It is distinct from assessing whether the scientific content or methodology is correct.
Reviewing deposits includes checking file formats, readability, file and folder structures, naming conventions, encoding, data types, dates, units, missing-value conventions, internal consistency, and the consistency between data and metadata. Corrupted, incomplete, duplicate, obsolete, or technically problematic files need to be identified, and dependencies and preservation risks need to be assessed. Request clarification or remediation from depositors where necessary. Apply appropriate automated validation and document any technical quality issues and actions taken.
text:
#### Sections
[Considerations](#considerations) | [Recommendations](#recommendations) | [More information](#more-information) | [Authors](#authors)

### Considerations

Key aspects to consider include:
 
- File integrity and readability (e.g. files can be opened and read without errors or corruption, checksums)
- File formats and sustainability (e.g. avoid obsolete, uncommon, proprietary formats)
- File structure and organisation (e.g. file and directory names are consistent and meaningful)
- Completeness of the deposited data (e.g. check that files required to understand and reuse the dataset are actually present)
- Internal consistency (e.g. inconsistent units of measurement, different coding schemes for categorical variables)
- Data structure and machine readability (e.g. consistent columns, consistent data types, valid syntax, references and identifiers resolve correctly)
- Character encoding and language (e.g. encoding is known and appropriate, preferably UTF-8 where suitable)
- Dates, numbers, units, and missing values
- Metadata-to-data consistency
- Versioning and provenance
- Compression and packaging (e.g. archives can be extracted)
- Technical documentation and dependencies (e.g. required software, libraries or packages)
- Automated validation and quality checks (e.g. file format identification, checksums/fixity, virus/malware scanning)
- Preservation risks (e.g. encrypted or password-protected files, unusual hardware/software dependencies, lossy compression)


### Recommendations

- Perform legal clearance and technical checks to make and keep data accessible.
- Data integrity should be ensured at all stages of its life.
- Data should be checked for technical defects and viruses prior to ingest.
- Data should be stored in well-supported and preferably non-proprietary file formats.
- Data should be well documented (e.g. clear explanations, standardized metadata, readme files).
- Datasets should be assigned unique identifiers.
- Updates to data or new versions should be clearly and consistently identified.


### More information

This module builds upon the following supporting frameworks:

- EOSC EDEN T1.2, Lindlar, M., Caron, B., Benauer, M., Kylander, J., Dekeyser, K., Addis, M., Levlin, M., Laukkanen, M., Lehtonen, J., Burger, F., Koho, T., Schwab, F., Molloy, L., & Zhang, F. (2025). EOSC EDEN M1.1 Report on Identification of Core Preservation Processes. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16992452 CPPs 001; 002; 003; 004; 007; 010; 012; 020; 023; 024; 025; 026; 027; 030

- CoreTrustSeal Standards and Certification Board. (2025). CoreTrustSeal Requirements 2026-2028. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17660463  R01; R03; R04

name: Preparing deposits - file formats and technical data quality
description: Considering data preservation and reusability during preparation helps ensure that the dataset remains accessible, understandable, and usable beyond the original research project. Good preparation—such as using sustainable formats, documenting data structures, and recording processing steps—reduces the risk of data becoming inaccessible, ambiguous, or unusable over time. It also makes it easier for other researchers to verify, reproduce, and build on the research.
text:
#### Sections:
[Considerations](#considerations) | [Recommendations](#recommendations) | [More information](#more-information) | [Authors](#authors)

### Considerations

Key aspects to consider include:
- Did you review the data you plan to deposit (e.g. are all necessary files included/unnecessary or redundant files removed? Which are raw, processed, derived, or final data?)  
- Are the file formats appropriate (e.g. widely used and supported, non-proprietary if possible)?
- Is technical file quality (e.g. files open correctly, completeness, coherent and clear file names) ok?
- Is the data machine-readable (e.g. consistent data types, consistent representations of missing values,  include units of measurement)?
- Did you use documented standards and conventions (e.g. units, geographic coordinates and reference systems, variable names and identifiers) commonly used in your scientific discipline?
- Is the data internally consistent (e.g. consistent variable names)?
- Is the data sufficiently and clearly explained and documented (e.g. readme file)?
Did you include provenance and processing information (e.g. processing scripts/documentation)?
Does the metadata reflect the actual files?


### Recommendations

- Check and follow the deposit guidelines of the repository you chose for your data deposit
- Familiarise yourself with (meta)data standards as well as conventions within your discipline and use them consistently
- Think about future re-use: does the dataset contain all necessary information by someone else?
